title: Can Parquet Floors Be Refinished? What Changes With the Pattern
meta: Yes, most parquet floors can be refinished at the same $3.99 per sq ft as strip oak. What changes is how the pattern is sanded. Wills Flooring, Seattle.
keywords: can parquet floors be refinished, refinishing parquet floors, sanding parquet flooring, parquet floor refinishing cost, herringbone floor refinish Seattle

blocks.lead: Yes. Solid parquet, including 1960s fingerblock tiles and 1920s herringbone, refinishes at the same $3.99 per sq ft as strip oak. The pattern changes the sanding method, not the price.
blocks.detail: Because the grain runs in several directions, parquet is sanded with a multi-disc machine rather than straight belt passes, and stain is riskier. Thin veneer parquet and loose or crumbling tiles are the exceptions.

blocks.html: Seattle has more parquet than people think. Capitol Hill and Queen Anne apartment buildings from the 1960s are full of 5/16-inch oak fingerblock tiles, Magnolia and Wallingford Tudors hide herringbone under wall-to-wall carpet, and plenty of 1950s ramblers have parquet in the entry. The question on the phone is always the same: can it be sanded like a normal floor, or does the pattern make it a tear-out? Usually it can. Here is what actually changes.

blocks.text: First, figure out which parquet you have

items.title: Solid fingerblock tiles
items.text: Squares of short oak strips glued in alternating directions, usually 5/16 in thick, laid in mastic on plywood or slab. Common in 1960s and 70s condos and apartments. Refinishes well two or three times over its life.

items.title: Solid herringbone or basket weave
items.text: Individual 3/4 in strips laid in a pattern, often in 1920s to 1940s Tudors and Colonials. Thick, tough and the best candidate for refinishing. Border strips and mitered corners just need care at the edges.

items.title: Engineered veneer parquet
items.text: A thin real-wood face, sometimes under 2 mm, over plywood. Common in 1980s and 90s installs. One careful sanding is usually possible; a floor already sanded once may only take a recoat.

items.title: Laminate or vinyl parquet look
items.text: Printed pattern on a laminate or vinyl core. Cannot be sanded. If a fingernail on an edge shows no wood grain and the tiles feel plastic, this is what you have.

blocks.text: How the pattern changes the sanding

items.text: We tap every tile. Hollow or rocking blocks are lifted, cleaned and re-glued, or replaced from salvaged stock. Sanding a loose tile shatters it.
On a belt or drum machine, the first cut runs diagonally to the pattern so no block is sanded across its grain at full aggression. On fragile floors we skip the belt entirely.

A planetary multi-disc sander does the medium and fine grits. Its heads spin in several directions at once, so alternating grain gets a uniform scratch pattern and no tile ends up with cross-grain marks.
items.note: This step is why parquet takes about half a day longer than a strip floor of the same size.

items.text: Gaps between blocks are filled, then a final buff with fine screen. Fill color is matched to the oak, not the finish.
Three coats of Bona water-based finish, same as any refinish. Satin hides the tiny grain-direction differences best.

blocks.text: Price your Seattle parquet floor right now

blocks.html: Parquet is billed at the same published rates as any hardwood. A 640 sq ft Capitol Hill condo with fingerblock parquet is 640 × $3.99 = $2,554 for a natural finish, or 640 × $6.50 = $4,160 stained. If your only problem is a dull, scratched finish over sound tiles, a screen and recoat at $1.99 per sq ft may be all you need.

blocks.note: Re-gluing loose tiles and replacing missing blocks are quoted on site after we tap the floor. Condo elevator and quiet-hour arrangements are sorted at the estimate.

blocks.text: When parquet should not be refinished

a.title: Good candidate when
items: Tiles are solid wood 5/16 in or thicker, or veneer with a face over 2 mm and never sanded
Fewer than about 5 percent of tiles are loose or missing
Damage is scratches, gray finish, sun fade or light pet stains
The floor is original to a 1920s to 1970s Seattle home and you want to keep it

b.title: Walk away when
items: Tiles lift by hand across large areas because the mastic has failed
Water from a leak has cupped whole sections and the plywood under them is soft
The veneer face is already worn through to plywood at doorways
It is laminate or vinyl that only looks like parquet

blocks.title: Seattle-specific warning:
blocks.text: Black mastic under parquet from the 1950s to 1970s may contain asbestos. It is safe left undisturbed under intact tiles, which is one more reason to refinish rather than tear out. If tiles have to come up, we stop and have the adhesive tested first.
Mistakes that ruin parquet during refinishing

items.html: Running a drum sander with the pattern. Half the blocks get sanded across the grain at full pressure. The result is deep cross-grain scratches that only show up once the finish goes on.
Taking too much wood. Fingerblock at 5/16 in has maybe two sandings in it. A crew that starts at 36 grit on a floor that only needs 60 has used up a future refinish.
Flooding the floor with water-pop or stain. Water gets into the gaps between blocks and can loosen old mastic. Parquet is dampened, not soaked.
Skipping the tap test. A loose tile under a sander turns into a hole. Every block gets checked before the first machine starts.
Filling gaps with the wrong product. Latex filler shrinks and falls out of parquet joints within a year. We use a wood-flour and finish slurry that flexes with the blocks.

blocks.text: What to check before you book

items: Confirm it is solid or thick-veneer wood: look at a tile edge at a heat register or closet, or ask us to check at the free estimate
Count loose, hollow-sounding or missing tiles; a handful is normal, whole rooms are a different conversation
If you live in a Capitol Hill, Queen Anne or Belltown condo, get the building's work-hours and elevator rules in writing before the crew is scheduled
Decide on sheen, and lean satin; parquet in gloss shows every tile edge
Ask how the crew will sand the pattern; the answer should include a multi-disc machine, not just a drum or belt
If gaps or a previous bad sanding are the worry, read how many sandings a floor has left before deciding
Get a written quote that lists the measured area, the rate, and re-gluing or replacement blocks as separate lines

faq.q: Does refinishing parquet cost more than refinishing regular hardwood?
faq.a: Not at Wills Flooring. Parquet is billed at the same published rates: $3.99 per sq ft natural, $6.50 with stain, $1.99 for a screen and recoat, 500 sq ft minimum. Re-gluing loose tiles or replacing missing ones is quoted separately after inspection.

Yes. The oak fingerblock in most Seattle condos and apartments is solid, about 5/16 in thick, and takes two or perhaps three careful sandings over its life. We check for loose tiles first and use a multi-disc sander for the fine cuts so the alternating grain stays even.

faq.q: Why does stained parquet look blotchy?
faq.a: Because neighboring blocks have grain running in different directions. End grain and quartersawn faces absorb more stain than flat grain, so tiles go darker or lighter than their neighbors. Natural finish avoids it. If you want color, we test stain on a few blocks first.

faq.q: Can loose parquet tiles be fixed during refinishing?
faq.a: Yes, if the number is small. Loose blocks are lifted, cleaned of old adhesive and re-glued before sanding. Missing blocks are replaced with matching salvaged oak. If tiles are lifting across whole rooms, the adhesive has failed and replacement is the honest answer.

faq.q: How long does refinishing a parquet floor take?
faq.a: About half a day longer than a strip floor of the same size, because the multi-disc passes are slower. A 600 to 900 sq ft parquet floor with a natural finish usually takes three to four days including cure time between coats. Stain adds a day.

faq.q: Is the black glue under old parquet dangerous?
faq.a: Black cutback mastic from before about 1980 may contain asbestos. It is not a hazard while the tiles stay down and intact, which refinishing preserves. We never scrape or grind it. If tiles must come up, we have the adhesive tested before any removal.
